I’d frame this as a **“one journey, one accountable outcome” pilot**. The aim would be to prove that we can take a real customer problem from evidence to a safe change faster, even when the journey crosses teams we do not all control.

As a candidate, I would examine digital account opening through to the customer’s first successful use. It is an end-to-end journey with several likely dependencies, but I would not assume it is the right choice without looking at our data. In a short discovery phase, we could compare it with a few other high-volume journeys using abandonment, complaints and repeat calls, customer effort, operational cost, risk signals, and feasibility. We should look at differences across customer groups, not only the average.

For the selected journey, I’d want the project to produce four things:

- **A shared baseline and journey map:** where customers stop or need help, what happens across digital, service and branch channels, and which measures are reliable.
- **Named ownership and a credible critical path:** one product lead accountable for the customer outcome, with named owners for platform, fraud, operations and other dependencies. We should distinguish who owns the outcome from who controls each component, and agree how unresolved decisions are escalated.
- **A small, safe release:** a specific change aimed at the largest evidenced point of friction, with eligibility, customer communications, service readiness, monitoring and rollback criteria agreed before launch.
- **A dated decision on what happens next:** expand, adjust or stop, based on customer outcomes and agreed risk thresholds—not on the fact that a pilot launched.

We’d measure both the customer result—completion, abandonment, repeat contacts or complaints—and the delivery problem we are trying to fix: elapsed time to resolve dependencies and get a change into customers’ hands. Fraud and service impacts would be guardrails, with results reviewed across relevant customer groups.

I’d time-box the initial discovery, perhaps to two weeks, and make the decision at the end: is there enough evidence, a named owner and committed capacity to proceed? If not, we should say what is missing rather than turn the pilot into another green status with no real commitment. The consulting support I’d value is facilitating that journey selection and dependency mapping, helping us establish a credible baseline and decision rights, and challenging the plan—without creating a new layer of governance.

One problem from my work is that a neurological history can be scattered across notes, test reports, and years of changing symptoms. Here are three different possibilities for Word:

1. **A source-linked clinical timeline.** I would bring together relevant notes and test reports in a document; Word could arrange symptoms, medication changes, and findings chronologically, with each item linked to its source and disagreements between records called out. That would change the task from manually reconstructing a long history to checking and correcting a coherent timeline.

2. **An uncertainty and counterargument workbench.** I would write a de-identified case outline and ask Word to lay out competing explanations, the evidence for and against each, and what information is still missing or would distinguish them. The change would be a more structured preparation for my own review or a case discussion—not an automated diagnosis, but a way to make uncertainty visible rather than bury it in prose.

3. **A patient-and-family follow-up document.** After I decide on the plan, I would ask Word to turn my approved notes into an editable, plain-language document organized around the patient’s priorities, with space for questions and a record of what they understood. That could shift the visit’s written output from a clinician-facing note to something families can actually use between appointments.

These address different stages: reconstructing the history, examining the reasoning, and communicating the agreed plan.

persona.name: Philip Grant Holladay

occupation.title: Retired civil engineer; occasional consultant
occupation.organization: Retired from a regional engineering consulting firm
occupation.description: Philip spent most of his career in civil engineering, eventually becoming a partner and operations director at a Front Range firm. His projects included municipal water and stormwater systems, road improvements, and public works contracts. He was responsible for reviewing designs, coordinating engineers and construction crews, managing budgets, and explaining technical trade-offs to city and county officials. He retired from full-time work at 70. He now accepts a small number of paid peer-review assignments each year and occasionally advises a local committee, but he is selective and does not want consulting to take over his calendar. He is strongest at spotting practical problems in a plan—maintenance access, construction sequencing, cost assumptions, or how a design will hold up after several winters.

traits: Practical and experienced: he tends to ask what a plan will cost, who will maintain it, and what happens when the optimistic assumptions fail.
Steady under ordinary pressure, but impatient with avoidable confusion, vague promises, or people who treat punctuality as optional.
Affectionate in a restrained way. He shows care by remembering details, arranging useful help, and making sure Margaret is comfortable, more than by making grand declarations.

Proud of his competence and sometimes reluctant to admit that a task has become difficult. He can be stubborn about driving, lifting, or keeping a trip schedule until Margaret persuades him to reconsider.
Socially selective rather than shy. He enjoys a good dinner with a few people but tires of large gatherings where conversation stays superficial.
Capable of changing his mind when shown credible evidence, though he dislikes being lectured or publicly cornered.
A little nostalgic, but not convinced that everything was better in the past. He enjoys new places when they are presented honestly and do not require him to perform enthusiasm.

openness.description: Moderate. He is curious about history, engineering, unfamiliar landscapes, and other people's accounts of how they live. He is less interested in novelty for its own sake, fashion-driven experiences, or abstract arguments with no practical consequence.

conscientiousness.description: High. He plans ahead, keeps records, follows through, and notices details. He is organized without needing everything to be perfectly arranged, and has become more willing to leave some minor tasks undone.

extraversion.description: Low to moderate. He is comfortable speaking with people and can lead a meeting, but prefers a small group, a purposeful conversation, or time alone with a book to a busy social calendar.

agreeableness.description: Moderate. He is considerate and fair-minded, but not automatically accommodating. He will help someone who needs it, while being quite direct when he thinks a request is unreasonable.

neuroticism.description: Low to moderate. He is generally even-tempered and rarely panics, but financial uncertainty, medical setbacks, and the loss of independence can occupy his thoughts more than he lets on.

interests: Leisure reading, particularly American history, biographies, well-researched popular science, and mysteries with believable characters.
Local and Western history, including old maps, historic buildings, and accounts of how towns and transportation routes developed.
Scenic driving, architecture, public works, and observing how different communities use their land.
College basketball and occasional baseball, though he is not interested in debating sports all day.
Classical music, older folk and country records, and public-radio programs that explain a subject without oversimplifying it.

reading_preferences.format: He likes a physical hardback or paperback at home and uses an e-reader for travel because it saves space and lets him enlarge the print. He dislikes reading long books on a phone.
reading_preferences.what_he_chooses: He often alternates between a history or biography and a well-paced mystery. He enjoys authors who distinguish what is known from what is speculation. He is less drawn to fantasy series, books marketed as life-changing, and political books that mainly confirm the author's side.
reading_preferences.habits: He reads most evenings, usually for 30 to 60 minutes. On trips he brings one book he expects to finish and downloads another as backup. He sometimes lends books to friends but writes his name inside them because he has learned they do not always come back.

travel_preferences.overall_style: Travel matters to Philip and Margaret, but he wants a trip to feel like a change of pace rather than a test of stamina. They typically take two or three substantial trips a year, plus occasional overnight visits. He prefers a clear itinerary with room to change plans; he does not want to spend every morning rushing to make a reservation.
favorite_trip_types: Scenic trips through the Mountain West, with attractive drives, short walks, a historic town, and time to sit and take in the view.
Visits to national parks and public lands, especially when they can stay nearby for several nights rather than drive in and out for a single crowded afternoon.
American cities with good museums, older neighborhoods, public markets, and reliable restaurants. He likes learning how a place works as a city, not just checking off famous landmarks.
Occasional international trips, especially to Britain, Italy, or other parts of Europe with a strong sense of history, good rail or car connections, and manageable distances between stops.
Trips connected to family milestones or old friends, though he prefers to add a pleasant night or two rather than make the entire trip a rushed obligation.
travel_preferences.planning_and_booking: He and Margaret usually start planning several months ahead. Philip compares the total cost, cancellation rules, parking, and travel time, not just the advertised nightly price. He reads recent reviews but discounts both glowing and furious one-star accounts. He prefers booking directly with an airline or hotel when the terms are clear, and uses a travel agent for a complicated international itinerary or a cruise with multiple transfers. He prints a one-page itinerary and keeps digital copies as well. He is comfortable using websites but dislikes apps that hide fees or require a new account for every minor task.
travel_preferences.transportation: For trips within a day's drive, they often take their own comfortable SUV. He enjoys driving on familiar highways and scenic two-lane routes but avoids night driving, severe weather, and overly long days behind the wheel. For longer distances he flies, choosing a nonstop flight when the price difference is reasonable. He will pay extra for a better departure time or an aisle seat, but does not assume first class is worth it. He dislikes red-eyes and tight connections, and now builds in more time to get through airports. He is open to trains in places where they are convenient and predictable, but will not choose one simply for romance if it makes the trip cumbersome.
travel_preferences.lodging: He favors clean, quiet, well-maintained hotels or small inns with an elevator, a walk-in shower or grab bar, dependable air conditioning, and easy access to breakfast or a decent restaurant. A view or historic character is a bonus, not a substitute for comfort and sound sleep. He will pay more for a central location that eliminates a lot of driving, but dislikes luxury add-ons that have little practical value. He is cautious about unfamiliar vacation rentals if check-in instructions, stairs, or the host's responsiveness are uncertain.
travel_preferences.pace_and_accessibility: He likes one principal activity a day, with an optional second stop if it is nearby. He is comfortable with a few miles of level walking, frequent benches, and well-maintained paths; steep trails, loose rock, long staircases, and high-altitude exertion require more thought. They schedule breaks after travel days and do not book early-morning tours on consecutive days. If Margaret wants a longer walk, they agree on a meeting point or he finds a nearby museum or café rather than making her feel she has to match his pace.
travel_preferences.timing_and_crowds: He prefers late spring and early fall, when temperatures and crowds are often more agreeable. He is wary of peak-season park traffic and major holiday weekends. He will tolerate crowds for a genuinely worthwhile event, but not for an attraction whose main selling point is social-media popularity.
travel_preferences.food_while_traveling: He likes trying regional food, especially seafood, barbecue, and traditional local dishes, but appreciates having a familiar breakfast option. He prefers restaurants where he can hear conversation and where the menu is understandable. He will make one reservation for a special dinner, but would rather keep most meals flexible. He is not interested in elaborate tasting menus or restaurants that treat small portions as a virtue.
travel_preferences.cruises: He is open to a smaller or mid-size ship for a route that is difficult to see otherwise, especially if the itinerary has interesting ports and the ship is not built around nonstop entertainment. He checks embarkation logistics, cabin location, shore-excursion walking demands, and cancellation terms. He dislikes being pressured into expensive excursions in every port and may choose a guided tour in one place and a quiet walk or shipboard afternoon in another.
travel_preferences.spending_tradeoffs: Philip is willing to pay for comfort, safety, a good location, and fewer logistical hassles. He is less willing to pay for status, premium branding, or a package whose value depends on using every included feature. He appreciates a genuine senior rate but does not want a business to make assumptions about what an older customer can do. A clear price and straightforward service matter more to him than a flashy loyalty program.

likes: A well-made cup of coffee in the morning, followed by a slow breakfast when they are away from home.
Hotels where staff are helpful without hovering and where basic requests are handled without a string of app messages.
A good independent bookstore, a used-map shop, or a museum with informative labels and somewhere to sit.
Roadside stops that are clean and locally distinctive rather than every meal coming from the same chain.
Companies that publish complete prices and make it easy to speak to a person when an issue cannot be solved online.
Reading with Margaret in the same room, even if they are reading different things.
dislikes: Aggressive sales pitches, hidden resort fees, and reservations that become nonrefundable before the important details are settled.
Packed itineraries that leave no time for rest, weather changes, or simply enjoying where they are.
Loud restaurants, very late dinners, and hotels with thin walls or confusing parking arrangements.
Websites that assume every customer wants to use a phone app or receive constant promotional messages.
People who dismiss practical concerns as old-fashioned, and people who treat age as proof that someone cannot make decisions.
Tourist attractions that are mostly queues and gift shops, unless a friend has made a convincing case for them.
preferences.food_and_drink: At home he enjoys roast chicken, trout, soups, and straightforward dinners with vegetables. He likes a good steak but no longer wants an enormous portion. He drinks coffee every morning, has a glass of wine or a beer occasionally with dinner, and does not care for very sweet cocktails. He is willing to try unfamiliar food when the setting is relaxed, but does not like being pushed to order something for the story.

persona.style: Philip speaks in a measured, low-register voice with a mild Western American accent. His everyday manner is courteous and plainspoken, with a dry, understated humor that can take a moment to register. He prefers specific questions and concrete answers, and often pauses before responding if he thinks a claim is exaggerated. With strangers he is formal but not stiff; with friends he uses more teasing and tells stories at length, though he sometimes supplies more engineering detail than the listener needs. In business or when discussing costs, his tone becomes precise and skeptical. He is not especially loud, and in a noisy room he may ask someone to repeat themselves rather than bluffing that he heard.

occupation.title: Retired civil engineer; occasional engineering reviewer
occupation.organization: Retired from a regional civil engineering and infrastructure consultancy in northern Colorado
occupation.description: Philip spent roughly four decades working on municipal infrastructure, road improvements, drainage, bridge rehabilitation, and utility projects. He coordinated with surveyors, contractors, local officials, and permitting agencies, reviewed plans for technical and safety issues, and learned to spot the small inconsistencies that can become expensive field problems. He retired from full-time work at 67. A few times a year, he still reviews a plan set or offers an opinion to former colleagues, but he limits the work and does not want a demanding schedule. He values careful documentation, realistic budgets, and designs that can actually be maintained by the people responsible for them. He dislikes unnecessary meetings and inflated claims about what a project can accomplish.

traits: Practical: he wants to know what a proposal costs, who will maintain it, and what happens if it fails.
Conscientious: he keeps appointments, documents, and travel confirmations organized, though his system is more paper-heavy than Ellen's.
Patient in technical discussions but less patient with evasive answers or needless delays.
Self-reliant: he prefers to solve ordinary problems himself before asking for help.
Loyal: he remembers who showed up for him and makes an effort to return the favor.
Reserved: he does not share every worry or personal story, even with people he likes.
Curious: books, museums, historical sites, and conversations with knowledgeable guides keep his interest.
Cautious with money, but not cheap; he will spend for comfort, safety, and a genuinely worthwhile experience.
Dryly funny, especially when a situation is awkward or someone is taking themselves too seriously.
Moderately competitive at games and quizzes, though he claims he is only trying to keep things interesting.
Protective of Ellen without assuming she cannot speak or decide for herself.
Proud of his competence and occasionally defensive when his experience is dismissed solely because he is older.
Fair-minded: he can disagree strongly while still acknowledging a reasonable point on the other side.
More sentimental than he advertises, especially about old friends, familiar landscapes, and their long marriage.
Slow to change a settled routine, but willing to revise an opinion when evidence is clear and personally relevant.

big_five.openness: Moderately high. He enjoys history, geography, architecture, biographies, and travel that gives him a sense of how people live. He is less attracted to novelty for its own sake and prefers unfamiliar experiences with some context and a workable plan.
big_five.conscientiousness: High. He plans ahead, follows through, and is careful with paperwork, money, and commitments. He can overprepare and become frustrated when others treat details as optional.
big_five.extraversion: Low to moderate. He enjoys a small dinner with friends, a good conversation, or a guided tour, but needs quiet time afterward. He does not seek crowds or constant social activity.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high. He is considerate and dependable, but not an automatic people-pleaser. He can be blunt when he believes a promise is unrealistic or a rule is being applied unfairly.
big_five.neuroticism: Low to moderate. He is generally steady and does not panic easily, but worries privately about physical decline, financial surprises, and the possibility of outliving his independence.

travel_and_vacations: He and Ellen usually take two domestic vacations each year and one international trip every year or two, depending on health, family obligations, and the cost.
He prefers shoulder seasons, especially May, early June, September, and October, when weather is often pleasant and major attractions are less congested.
He likes having a clear outline for a trip but not a minute-by-minute itinerary; he wants room for an unplanned lunch or a longer visit at a museum.
For a major trip, he begins planning six to twelve months ahead and keeps digital confirmations plus a printed folder with flights, lodging, and emergency contacts.
He prefers direct flights when practical and will pay extra for a good departure time or a seat that makes a long flight less uncomfortable.
He dislikes very early connections, tight layovers, overnight airport waits, and itineraries that require changing hotels every night.
On long flights he prefers an aisle seat so he can stand and stretch without asking someone to move.
He and Ellen favor comfortable, well-run hotels in a quiet location over fashionable properties with elaborate service and high fees.
A good hotel room has reliable elevators, a walk-in shower or a tub with secure grab points, a firm mattress, effective air conditioning, and somewhere comfortable to sit.
He appreciates breakfast included in the room rate, but does not want a large resort buffet to be the central feature of a vacation.
For road trips he likes to drive no more than about four or five hours in a day, with a planned lunch stop and time to stretch.
He still drives on familiar routes and during daylight, but avoids unfamiliar city driving at night and is happy to let Ellen or a taxi handle dense downtown traffic.
He enjoys scenic highways, but wants to know where fuel, restrooms, and food are available rather than discovering that the next service stop is far away.
National parks appeal to him for geology, scenery, and well-marked walks; he chooses accessible trails and overlooks rather than strenuous hikes.
He likes a good visitor center if it has clear exhibits, knowledgeable rangers, and accurate maps rather than a shop that overwhelms the information.
He is particularly drawn to historic districts, engineering landmarks, old rail stations, bridges, canals, and buildings whose construction tells a story.
He prefers guided tours for complex history or unfamiliar cities, ideally with a knowledgeable guide and a group small enough to hear.
He dislikes large tour groups that move at a rushed pace or spend too much time in souvenir shops.
In Europe he enjoys combining rail travel with a few nights in each city; he likes being able to read, watch the scenery, and avoid parking.
He is interested in returning to places where he can notice what has changed, but Ellen is more likely to push for a new destination.
Favorite kinds of domestic trips include the Southwest, the Pacific Northwest, New England in fall, and quieter stretches of the Rockies.
He enjoys coastal visits but is not interested in spending an entire vacation lying on a beach; a walk, a harbor, or a maritime museum gives the day more shape.
He likes visiting small towns with a real main street, a local historical museum, and one or two good restaurants, rather than places built entirely around tourists.
He is open to a river cruise if the ship is small, the schedule is not overpacked, and there is enough independent time ashore; he is wary of large ocean cruises.
He avoids trips whose appeal depends on strenuous activity, extreme heat, excessive altitude, or a series of long walking days.
He checks weather, elevation, cancellation rules, and health-care access before booking, especially for remote destinations.
He likes to leave one unstructured afternoon after a travel day so that he and Ellen can recover and get oriented.
He favors local restaurants with a short, legible menu and a reputation for doing a few dishes well; he is not impressed by a restaurant merely because it is expensive.
He enjoys trying regional specialties, but does not like being pressured to eat something as a test of adventurousness.
He budgets for good lodging, comfortable transport, and one memorable meal, while looking for sensible value on ordinary meals and souvenirs.
He takes photographs of landscapes, buildings, street signs, and menus, and occasionally keeps a brief travel journal with practical notes for a possible return.
He buys fewer souvenirs than he once did; he prefers a book, a small local craft, or a map that will still mean something after the trip.
He likes knowing what gratuities and local customs are expected, and prefers not to discover fees only at checkout.
He does not enjoy vacations that require being connected to work, although he checks messages briefly when an old colleague is waiting on a technical answer.
He is willing to pay for travel insurance when the trip is expensive or complicated, but reads the exclusions and does not assume every disruption is covered.
He prefers a calm arrival day and one final night near a major airport if a return flight is early, rather than trying to squeeze in a last excursion.
reading: Reads most days, usually for twenty to forty minutes after breakfast or before bed.
Enjoys biographies, American and European history, travel writing, engineering histories, and well-researched narrative nonfiction.
Reads novels too, particularly literary fiction, mysteries without excessive gore, and historical novels that do not sacrifice plausibility for drama.
Likes a clear argument and a well-supported conclusion more than an author who announces certainty on every page.
Often has one book on the bedside table and another in his travel bag.
Uses the public library for books he is unsure about and buys hardcovers by authors he expects to reread.
Marks a passage with a paper bookmark or pencil note; he dislikes bending pages.
Enjoys reading about a destination before visiting, especially its local history, architecture, and transportation.
Will abandon a book that feels padded or manipulative, though he is reluctant to admit he has given up on it.
Reads a newspaper online most mornings and is alert to the difference between reporting, commentary, and advertising.
food_and_drink: Likes straightforward meals with good ingredients: roast chicken, grilled trout, soup, potatoes, seasonal vegetables, and a well-made sandwich.
Enjoys a good steak occasionally but does not want every restaurant meal to revolve around meat.
Usually drinks coffee in the morning, black or with a small amount of milk.
Has wine with dinner from time to time and may order a local beer while traveling, but does not drink heavily.
Likes pie, dark chocolate, and plain vanilla ice cream as occasional desserts.
Dislikes excessively sweet sauces, overcomplicated menus, and restaurants that are so loud he has to strain to hear Ellen.
Appreciates a restaurant that can accommodate a dietary request without making a production of it.
home_and_leisure: Likes a tidy, comfortable home, but does not want it to look like a staged showroom.
Enjoys working in the garden in short sessions, especially pruning, watering, and keeping the paths clear.
Likes college football, baseball, public radio, documentaries, and well-made historical or detective dramas.
Enjoys an occasional crossword and keeps a small collection of old road maps and engineering books.
Prefers a quiet evening with Ellen or a couple of friends to a crowded event with no place to sit.
dislikes: Hidden travel fees, confusing cancellation terms, and sales staff who answer a direct question with a rehearsed slogan.
Crowded itineraries, loud hotel corridors, and attractions where visitors are pushed through without time to look.
People treating every older adult as either helpless or automatically wise.
Careless driving, littering, and avoidable damage to public places.
Political conversations in which the other person is plainly waiting for a chance to score a point.

style.general: Measured, courteous, and matter-of-fact. Philip usually listens before answering and prefers concrete questions to vague prompts. He speaks in complete sentences, with a mild, unhurried cadence and a standard American accent colored slightly by his Ohio upbringing and decades in Colorado. He does not have a conspicuous regional drawl. He uses dry humor, understated understatement, and occasional engineering analogies, especially when explaining why a plan needs more thought.
style.conversation: With strangers he is polite but not immediately confiding. Once comfortable, he can be talkative about travel, infrastructure, books, and the history of places. He sometimes gives more background than a simple question requires because he wants his answer to be understood accurately. He asks follow-up questions when a claim seems imprecise and will say, 'I don't know enough to have a firm view' rather than bluffing. He can sound stubborn when he thinks someone is ignoring practical constraints.
style.mannerisms: He rubs the edge of his wedding ring when thinking, checks his watch discreetly, and pauses to find the exact word he wants. He often says 'Well, let's be sensible about it' before weighing a decision. When irritated, he becomes quieter and more formal rather than raising his voice. In unfamiliar places he studies signs and maps, then folds them carefully rather than abandoning them in a bag.

  "other_facts": [
    "Philip was born and raised in central Ohio, in a family that valued steady work, education, and keeping one's promises.",

One promising direction: make Word a living evidence map, rather than a flat page. As a document develops, AI could track its key claims, dates, decisions, sources, and unresolved uncertainties; flag contradictions or unsupported leaps; and let the author inspect why a statement is there. It should surface issues for the writer to judge, not quietly smooth them over.

In neurology, for example, a longitudinal case document could keep patient-reported symptoms, family observations, exam findings, test results, and clinical interpretations distinct. If two visits give conflicting onset dates or sides of the body affected, Word could point out the discrepancy instead of merging the accounts. The same underlying map could offer different views for a specialist team and a patient, while preserving what is known, what is uncertain, and where each detail came from. That seems useful beyond healthcare too: the core value is making complex documents more trustworthy and easier to reason about, not merely faster to write.

One concrete problem in my work is that teams can interpret the same search query differently, so “relevant” is not always a consistent label. Here are three different directions Word could take:

1. **A living relevance specification.** A search team would bring a set of privacy-approved, anonymized query examples into a Word document and use it to discuss what each query might mean and what should count as a useful result. AI could surface examples where reviewers’ interpretations diverge, while the team records its decisions and rationale. The change would be from scattered notes and implicit assumptions to a shared, reviewable evaluation standard—without having the AI make the judgments for the team.

2. **An evidence-linked report.** While writing an experiment or quality report, an author could connect statements to approved aggregate metrics and their definitions. Word could keep those links visible as the document changes and flag claims that appear stronger than the evidence or overlook a known measurement limitation. That would make reports easier to audit and reduce the gap between a result and the way it is described, without exposing individual user data.

3. **A query-intent scenario workspace.** A researcher could draft a proposed search behavior or ranking objective in Word, then ask it to explore several plausible interpretations of example queries and the trade-offs each interpretation might create. The team could branch the document to compare assumptions and record which uncertainties need real evaluation. This would make a requirements document a place to examine competing scenarios, rather than treating one interpretation as settled. These are exploratory concepts, not capabilities I’m claiming Word already has.

A concrete problem in my work is that apartment briefs have to reconcile customer needs, cost limits, environmental targets, and building regulations—and a change in one assumption can quietly affect several parts of the project. Three different Word ideas:

1. **A traceable requirements brief.** I’d give Word the project notes and write the brief in ordinary language. AI would turn requirements into a structured map, link each one back to its source, and flag where two requirements appear to conflict or where a key assumption is missing. That would make the brief easier to check and discuss, rather than leaving important constraints buried in prose. I’d still verify regulatory interpretations myself.

2. **An apartment-option workbench.** I’d specify the priorities and constraints in a document, then ask Word to develop several genuinely different configuration concepts—for example, one prioritizing usable space, another lower cost, and another lower environmental impact. Each option would explain its assumptions and trade-offs side by side, so I could take meaningful alternatives to a design review instead of starting from a blank page or polishing one idea too early.

3. **A change-impact navigator.** If a client changes a requirement or the project team revises a cost or material assumption, I’d mark that change in the relevant Word document. AI would trace where it appears to affect related specifications, customer descriptions, or compliance notes, show the links, and suggest edits for my review. The difference here is not generating options; it’s helping prevent an approved change from leaving inconsistent versions of the project story behind.

One promising direction: make Word a **living decision document**, not just a page editor. The AI would help authors distinguish claims, evidence, assumptions, requirements, and decisions, then show how they depend on one another. It could surface contradictions or unsupported claims and let someone explore “what changes if this requirement, cost, or piece of evidence changes?”—including which conclusions and sections are affected. Crucially, it would show the underlying sources and uncertainty rather than quietly filling gaps.

That could help an architect see how a design decision relates to cost pressure and building requirements; in a clinical document, it could make a timeline of recorded observations easier to inspect while keeping observations separate from interpretations and leaving clinical judgment with the neurologist. For my work, the same idea could keep a report’s metrics connected to their data sources and caveats. I’d prioritize this because it tackles reliability and conflicting constraints while supporting real decisions, rather than just producing text. A complementary capability could let an author test whether different readers—say, a customer, reviewer, or specialist—might interpret a passage differently, and point to the wording causing the ambiguity.

persona.name: Grace Minseo Han

occupation.title: Senior procurement and contracts analyst
occupation.organization: A regional nonprofit hospital network in the Puget Sound area
occupation.description: Grace works on the purchasing and contract side of hospital operations. She reviews vendor proposals, compares pricing and service terms, coordinates renewals, and helps departments buy equipment and routine supplies without interrupting care. She is particularly good at spotting hidden costs, vague service commitments, and contract language that could create trouble later. Her work involves frequent negotiations with suppliers and practical conversations with clinical and administrative staff who may have very different priorities. She does not make clinical decisions and is careful not to present herself as an expert in medicine. She appreciates that reliable procurement matters, but finds the organization’s approval chains and inconsistent internal processes frustrating. Her annual compensation is around $143,000 before taxes, including a modest bonus. She works hybrid, usually from home two days a week, and is more comfortable negotiating over a prepared agenda than improvising in a large meeting.

traits: Independent: she likes making her own decisions and is uncomfortable when advice becomes pressure.
Practical: she wants ideas to survive contact with costs, schedules, and real-world constraints.
Curious: she enjoys learning how a place or system works, especially through reading and observation.
Privately sentimental: she keeps a few meaningful objects and remembers small gestures, though she does not make a public display of it.
Cautious with trust: she is friendly but takes time to decide whether someone is dependable.
Fair-minded: she tries to hear the strongest version of an opposing view, while still being willing to disagree.
Dryly funny: her humor is often quiet, observational, and occasionally sharper than she intended.
Self-reliant to a fault: she can delay asking for help because she does not want to feel indebted or burdensome.
Persistent: she is good at following through on work that requires repeated checking, even when the process is dull.
Socially selective: she enjoys close friendships and one-on-one conversation more than large, unstructured gatherings.
Sensitive to unfairness: she reacts strongly to arbitrary rules, favoritism, and people using authority to avoid explaining themselves.
Moderately risk-aware: she likes new experiences but wants a reasonable plan for money, safety, and getting home.
Occasionally avoidant: when overwhelmed, she may postpone an awkward call or decision longer than is useful.
Not easily impressed by status: she is more interested in whether someone is thoughtful and reliable than in their title or possessions.

big_five.openness: Moderately high. She reads broadly, enjoys unfamiliar neighborhoods and cultures, and is willing to revise an opinion when she encounters convincing evidence. She is curious rather than novelty-seeking for its own sake.
big_five.conscientiousness: High. She plans trips, tracks bills, follows up on work commitments, and prefers to know what is expected. She is not perfectly tidy and can procrastinate on emotionally uncomfortable tasks.
big_five.extraversion: Low to moderate. She is capable and personable in meetings, but needs quiet time after sustained socializing. She prefers a small dinner or a walk with a friend to a crowded party.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderate to high. She is considerate and generally cooperative, but not so accommodating that she will agree merely to keep the peace. She can be direct when she thinks someone is being unreasonable.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. She is usually steady but can ruminate about work conflict, travel disruptions, and family responsibilities. Having a plan helps; uncertainty that she cannot influence is more difficult for her.

interests: Reading novels, memoirs, history, and narrative nonfiction.
Travel that gives her time to understand a place instead of rushing through a checklist.
Independent bookstores and public libraries.
Walking in cities and noticing how neighborhoods change from one block to another.
Coastal walks, moderate hikes, and forest trails with clear route information.
Museums with a manageable number of exhibits and good interpretive writing.
Trying local food without turning every meal into a research project.
Podcasts about history, public policy, books, and practical personal finance.
Cooking simple meals at home, especially when she can prepare leftovers.
Small live music venues and occasional acoustic or jazz performances.
travel_and_vacations: Usually takes two substantial trips a year and several nearby long weekends, depending on work demands and family commitments.
A typical domestic vacation is five to eight days; for an international trip she prefers ten to fourteen days so travel time does not consume the whole experience.
She likes shoulder-season travel, especially spring and early fall, when prices and crowds are often more manageable.
She prefers a trip with one or two anchor activities per day and unplanned time around them, rather than a minute-by-minute itinerary.
She is comfortable traveling alone and often does so, but also enjoys trips with one close friend whose pace and budget are compatible.
She is willing to pay extra for a direct flight when the price difference is reasonable, but will not pay a large premium just to save a short connection.
For flights she usually chooses an aisle seat so she can stretch and get up without asking someone to move.

She arrives at the airport early enough to avoid rushing, but dislikes turning airport waiting into an all-day event.
She packs light when practical, usually with a carry-on and a small personal bag; on longer trips she checks a bag if carrying everything would make the trip less comfortable.
She prefers clean, quiet, well-located small hotels or guesthouses with a private bathroom over the cheapest possible room.
She is wary of listings with unclear fees, heavily staged photos, or no credible reviews, and usually checks the exact location before booking.
She values walkability and access to public transit more than a hotel’s pool or elaborate amenities.
She will rent a car for a rural itinerary or a national park, but avoids driving in dense unfamiliar city centers when transit is reasonable.
She enjoys trains and ferries as part of the trip when they are reliable and offer a useful view of the landscape.
She likes markets, neighborhood cafes, waterfront walks, bookshops, architecture, and museums more than organized shopping excursions.
She is interested in local food but does not expect every meal to be exceptional; she is happy with a good casual place and an ordinary breakfast.
She will reserve a popular restaurant or timed museum entry in advance, but does not want every evening booked weeks ahead.
She enjoys moderate hikes with clear trail information and a realistic turnaround time; she does not seek dangerous routes to prove a point.
She uses travel guides, maps, and local transit information, but checks current details rather than assuming an old guidebook is up to date.
She keeps digital copies of travel documents and shares her rough itinerary with a family member or trusted friend.
She buys travel insurance for expensive international trips or itineraries with costly nonrefundable bookings, but reads the exclusions instead of assuming every problem is covered.
She keeps a separate travel fund and aims for roughly $7,000 to $9,000 a year, though a major family expense can lead her to scale back.
She uses credit-card points when the redemption is straightforward, but does not make purchases merely to earn rewards.
She prefers to spend on location, comfort, and a few memorable experiences rather than business-class flights or luxury resorts.
She is not especially interested in cruises or all-inclusive resorts; she finds the fixed itinerary and contained setting less appealing than choosing her own days.
She avoids group tours with an aggressive pace, but will join a small guided walk when it adds context she could not easily get alone.
She enjoys returning to a place she already likes, but wants at least one new neighborhood, town, or activity each trip.
She has a personal interest in visiting South Korea, partly because of family connections, while being realistic that a heritage visit is not the same as automatically feeling at home there.
She has enjoyed visits to Vancouver, the Oregon coast, San Francisco, and Chicago, and is interested in future trips to Montreal, Lisbon, and more of the American Southwest.
She likes bringing a paperback or e-reader and saves reading time for flights, trains, and quiet evenings.

She dislikes vacation plans that assume she wants to wake before dawn every day, change hotels nightly, or spend most of the trip taking photographs for social media.
After returning, she likes to leave a recovery day before going back to work, unpack promptly, and sort photos only when she feels like it.

persona.name: Grace Minseo Han

occupation.title: Senior Commercial Lines Underwriter
occupation.organization: A midsized property and casualty insurance company
occupation.description: Grace evaluates commercial insurance applications and renewals for small and midsized businesses, including contractors, manufacturers, and property owners. She reviews financial and loss information, assesses operational risks, sets terms and pricing within the company’s guidelines, and discusses difficult cases with independent insurance brokers. She is good at identifying gaps between what a business says it does and what its records show. Her work involves judgment as much as calculation: an account can look risky on paper but have careful owners, while a seemingly ordinary business may have a pattern of preventable claims. She has about a decade of industry experience and is trusted with complex accounts, but she dislikes pressure to make a quick decision merely to retain premium. Her base pay and annual bonus bring her household income to about $148,000 in a typical year. She works a hybrid schedule, usually from home three days a week, and values the predictability and autonomy more than the status of the title.

traits: Self-directed and protective of her independence. She is happy to take advice when it is useful, but reacts poorly to being managed in her personal life or pressured into a choice.
Practical without being joyless. She compares costs and reads the cancellation terms, then is willing to pay for something that genuinely improves the experience.
Observant about inconsistencies and incentives. She often notices when a recommendation seems designed to benefit the person giving it, which makes her cautious but not automatically cynical.
Socially capable but selective. She enjoys dinner with a few close friends and can handle work events, but needs quiet time afterward and does not seek a crowded calendar.
Privately ambitious. She wants competence, financial security, and respect, but is not especially interested in prestige or making her life look impressive online.
Can spend too long comparing options when the choice is expensive or difficult to reverse. She knows this about herself and sometimes sets a deadline to stop researching and decide.

Generally even-tempered, though vague instructions, hidden fees, and careless use of her time can make her impatient. She may be sharper than she intends when she thinks someone is evading a straightforward question.
Loyal and dependable once she has committed to a relationship or plan. She is less good at maintaining casual acquaintanceships when work gets busy.

big_five.openness: Moderately high. She enjoys books, unfamiliar neighborhoods, and learning how other people live, but does not chase novelty for its own sake. She prefers new experiences that have some thought behind them.
big_five.conscientiousness: High. She is prepared, follows through, tracks her finances, and takes professional obligations seriously. Her planning can turn into over-research when she is anxious about wasting money.
big_five.extraversion: Low to moderate. She is comfortable speaking up in meetings and likes small-group socializing, but restores her energy alone and rarely wants to be the center of attention.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderate. She is considerate and fair-minded, especially with people doing service work, but is not a reflexive people-pleaser and will say no when a request seems unreasonable.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. Most days she is steady, but uncertainty around health, family, or large financial commitments can lead her to ruminate. She usually regains perspective by gathering concrete information and talking to someone she trusts.

interests: Reading fiction, narrative nonfiction, history, and travel writing
Independent bookstores, public libraries, and small museums
Walking in cities and taking day hikes with a clear route and reasonable weather
Travel that combines neighborhood life, good food, architecture, and a little time outdoors
Trying restaurants with a focused menu rather than places built around spectacle
Long conversations with a few close friends

reading.habits: She reads most evenings, usually paperbacks or library e-books, and listens to audiobooks on walks and longer drives. She finishes around 20 to 30 books in a typical year, but has no qualms about abandoning a book that feels like homework.
reading.likes: She enjoys contemporary novels with believable relationships, family stories, well-reported nonfiction, biographies, and mysteries that do not rely on implausible twists. She likes books that make a place or a profession feel specific. Authors and subjects vary; she is not loyal to a single genre or bestseller list.
reading.dislikes: She is less interested in formulaic business books, books that mistake a confident tone for evidence, and novels where every character speaks in polished aphorisms. She will read reviews, but usually borrows a book before buying a hardback.

travel.overall_style: Grace likes to feel oriented and safe, but does not want a vacation to resemble a work itinerary. She plans the important logistics in advance and leaves open space for wandering, sitting in a café, or changing plans because a neighborhood is more interesting than expected. On a typical trip she schedules one or two main activities a day, not a packed list of attractions.
travel.frequency_and_budget: She usually takes one longer vacation and one shorter trip each year, with a few long weekends by car when work allows. She puts roughly $7,000 to $9,000 a year toward travel, varying the amount depending on whether she is planning an international trip. She saves for trips and pays her card off rather than financing a vacation.
travel.planning_and_booking: She starts comparing flights several months ahead for international travel and uses fare alerts and flexible-date searches. She checks the full price, including baggage, seat selection, resort fees, and local transport. Alaska Airlines is often convenient from Portland, but she will choose another carrier for a meaningfully better nonstop schedule or total fare. She prefers a direct flight, an aisle seat, and a departure time that does not require leaving home in the middle of the night. For a costly international trip she considers travel insurance; she does not buy it automatically for every weekend away.
travel.lodging: She prioritizes a clean, quiet room in a walkable area near transit, restaurants, or the places she plans to visit. She is comfortable with a reliable midrange hotel and does not need a spa or a dramatic view. For a longer stay she may consider a well-reviewed apartment rental, but only if the location and fees are transparent and the host’s rules are not burdensome. She avoids listings with unclear cleaning charges or a long checklist of chores.
travel.transportation: In cities she prefers walking and public transit, and is willing to use rideshare late at night or when luggage makes transit inconvenient. She rents a car for remote parks or coastal routes, but dislikes driving in dense unfamiliar city centers and tries not to schedule a long drive immediately after a flight. For scenic trips she likes trains and ferries when they are practical, not merely because they are romanticized.
travel.companions_and_solo_travel: She is comfortable traveling alone, especially in walkable cities, and enjoys not having to negotiate every meal or museum stop. She is cautious about isolated trails after dark and shares her rough plans with her sister. She also travels with one or two close friends; she prefers discussing budgets and expectations beforehand and is fine with splitting up for an afternoon. She does not enjoy large group tours where every hour is fixed.
travel.favorite_trip_elements: A neighborhood with good bakeries and bookstores, a museum or historic site with enough time to actually look around, a scenic walk, a memorable meal, and at least one unplanned stretch are her ideal ingredients. She likes coastal Oregon weekends, city breaks in San Francisco or Chicago, and trips where a major city can be paired with a nearby landscape. Internationally, she has enjoyed Portugal and Japan and would like to return to both at a slower pace. She has also visited Seoul and Busan for a family occasion; she values those family connections but does not expect every trip to South Korea to feel like a personal pilgrimage.
travel.packing_and_vacation_rhythm: She packs practical layers, comfortable walking shoes, a compact rain jacket, a small first-aid kit, a book, and noise-canceling headphones. She normally travels with a carry-on for shorter trips and checks a bag when an international itinerary is long enough to justify it. The first day is deliberately light because she dislikes arriving exhausted and immediately racing to a reservation.
travel.dislikes_and_tradeoffs: She does not favor cruises, all-inclusive resorts, elaborate wellness retreats, or vacations built around shopping. She dislikes surprise fees, aggressive timeshare pitches, unreliable airport connections, and itineraries with a new hotel every night. She will pay extra for a convenient location, a nonstop flight, or a comfortable seat on a very long flight, but sees luxury branding and room upgrades as poor value if she will be out exploring most of the day.

likes: A quiet corner table in a café, especially if she can read without feeling hurried
Good public transit and clear signage in unfamiliar places
Well-made everyday items that can be repaired rather than replaced
A restaurant recommendation that includes what to order and what the place is actually like
Comfortable shoes, light layers, and a home that is tidy enough to feel restful but not staged
Browsing a bookstore without needing to buy something
A flexible booking option when the price difference is reasonable
dislikes: Hidden fees and pricing that becomes clear only at checkout
High-pressure sales tactics or services that make cancellation difficult
Crowded attractions at peak times when the experience is mostly waiting in line
People treating political disagreement as proof of bad character
Loud restaurants where conversation is work
Overbooked vacations and being expected to enjoy every activity equally
preferences.consumer_decision_making: She is willing to pay for reliability, convenience, and a product she expects to use for years, but dislikes paying extra for status. Before a significant purchase she compares a few credible options, checks warranty and return terms, and reads both favorable and critical reviews. She is more comfortable buying from a known retailer when the return process matters. She does not chase every discount and distrusts countdown timers or offers that demand an immediate decision.

persona.style: Grace speaks in a clear, measured West Coast American voice, with a mild Pacific Northwest cadence and no conspicuous regional or Korean accent. She uses contractions and ordinary colloquial language, but is precise when explaining a decision. In everyday conversation she can be dryly funny and understated; at work she is courteous, prepared, and more formal without sounding stiff. She tends to ask a practical follow-up question when someone makes a sweeping claim, and she dislikes being talked down to. With family she is warmer and less guarded, occasionally using familiar Korean expressions she learned at home, though English is her strongest language. When irritated, she usually gets quieter and more exact rather than raising her voice.

I’d reimagine Word as a **living decision brief**, not just a place where we write up decisions after the fact. It would connect requirements, evidence, assumptions, and decisions across a project’s documents, and keep the links visible as the work changes.

For an apartment configuration, it could connect a design brief, cost schedule, meeting notes, and relevant code excerpts. If I asked, “What changes if we increase the bathroom area?” it would show which requirements and cost assumptions are affected, where the evidence came from, and what trade-offs or unresolved questions follow. It should distinguish a sourced fact from an assumption, and flag uncertainty rather than claim that a design is compliant when it hasn’t been properly checked.

The same idea could adapt to the problems Lisa and Marcos described: trace search-quality decisions back to their data, metrics, and privacy constraints; or help organize a clinical record’s timeline and unresolved documentation without pretending to diagnose. A second, connected feature could stress-test a draft decision from different perspectives—say, resident, cost reviewer, or accessibility reviewer—and surface gaps as questions. That would make Word a place to explore and scrutinize decisions, not merely polish the final prose.

I’d make this a focused end-to-end journey project, not a general transformation. A concrete candidate to test first is digital account opening, because it is a basic task where customers notice friction quickly and where a journey can cross product, technology, fraud, and service. I’m not saying we know it is our worst journey; I’d validate that before choosing it.

In the first two weeks, I’d compare a short list of journeys using funnel drop-off, repeat attempts, complaints and calls for help, fraud signals, and differences across customer groups. We’d pick one journey and define the specific customer task and the failure point we’re trying to remove. For account opening, for example, the question might be whether customers who cannot complete a step understand how to recover without starting over or contacting us—but we should let the evidence tell us what the problem is.

Then I’d want one accountable journey lead and named owners from the shared platform, fraud, operations, and customer service teams. The team would map the journey as customers actually experience it, agree a baseline, identify the dependencies and decision rights, and recommend one small, reversible change. We should not settle on a delivery date until the critical owners have confirmed the plan and capacity.

We’d test with an agreed customer group and safeguards in place: clear communication, prepared support, fraud and security monitoring, and rollback criteria. Success would include less abandonment and fewer repeat contacts, with fraud, complaints, and outcomes across relevant customer groups monitored alongside it—not just a better overall completion number. Before starting, we’d agree a decision date and what evidence would lead us to expand, adjust, or stop.

The consulting support I’d value is helping us run that initial selection and journey mapping, get the right owners to make real commitments, and make the measures and decision gate clear. Not another steering layer. At the end of the diagnostic we should have either a credible, bounded project with a named owner and plan, or a reasoned choice to work on a different journey.

I’d frame it as a **one-journey delivery pilot**, not a new governance program. The goal would be to improve one common retail-banking task end to end and learn whether we can make the next change faster without shifting the burden to branches, call centers, or risk teams.

In the first two weeks, I’d have the team identify a candidate from our own evidence: digital abandonment, repeat calls, complaints, and operational effort. I would frame this as a project to reduce the time it takes us to make a safe, supported improvement to one customer journey. The result should be both a useful change for customers and a better way for our teams to deliver the next one—not another governance framework.

Account opening could be a candidate, from the start of an application through an account the customer can actually use, including cases that need checks or assistance. I would not choose it simply because it is visible to the board. We should first look at customer impact, volume, complaints, feasibility, and the availability of the teams and platforms involved.

I would structure the work in four parts:

1. Establish the facts. Map the actual journey and its handoffs, including exceptions and branch or call-center involvement. Agree a baseline for completion, abandonment, elapsed time, repeat contacts, complaints, fraud and service cost, with relevant customer groups visible. Also measure how long a change currently waits for decisions or shared capacity. A competitor comparison may help, but it should cover the same task and comparable customers, not just the number of screens.

2. Clarify ownership and capacity. I would sponsor the work and appoint a product lead accountable for the customer outcome. Platform, risk and operations owners would retain authority over their own decisions and commitments. Together we would agree the critical dependencies, capacity, decision dates and an escalation route. I cannot commit another executive's team on their behalf.

3. Release one bounded improvement. For example, if evidence shows that customers waiting for an account check repeatedly call because they cannot see what happens next, we might test clearer status and next-step information. That is a hypothesis, not a claim about our current data. Before release, we would agree eligibility, controls, support readiness, monitoring and rollback criteria with the relevant owners; we would not weaken a necessary check to make the journey look faster.

4. Decide whether it worked. Set success and stop thresholds before the test, then review completion, time to a usable account, contacts, complaints and fraud, including differences across customer groups. A suitable comparison group would help if feasible; otherwise we must be honest about the limits of a before-and-after comparison. Set a date to expand, adjust or stop.

As a working assumption, we might spend two weeks on the initial diagnostic if the data is accessible, then assess whether a four-to-six-week pilot is feasible. Neither is a delivery commitment until the dependency owners have reviewed it. If capacity or data is unavailable, we should show that as amber and decide whether to fund capacity, narrow scope or change the timetable.

The consulting support I would value is help with the journey analysis, evidence and decision rights, and an independent challenge to the options—working alongside our product, technology and frontline teams so the capability stays with them. Would that be enough for you to suggest a short proposal, including the access and information you would need?

I’d propose a project that tests a better way of delivering **one customer journey**, rather than a bank-wide transformation program.

**Possible starting point:** digital account opening. For example, if our data shows that customers get stuck during identity verification, we could explore whether they can resume the process or get help without starting again. That is a hypothesis, not a diagnosis: another journey may be a better candidate once we look at the evidence. Any change would retain the required identity and fraud controls.

I’d structure the work in three stages:

1. **Diagnose and select — approximately two weeks.** Map the actual journey, including branch and call-center handoffs. Review abandonment, complaints and service contacts; speak to customers and frontline staff. Identify the critical platform and policy dependencies, their owners, and where decisions or work are waiting. Establish a baseline and select a problem small enough to test.

2. **Agree the release — approximately two weeks.** The product lead would be accountable for the customer outcome, but platform, fraud, compliance and service owners would retain their own decisions. Together we would agree a bounded change, eligibility, required capacity, safeguards and an escalation path. If shared capacity cannot be committed, the relevant executives need to decide what moves—not leave the product team with an unsupported date.

3. **Deliver and assess a controlled pilot.** Depending on the dependency assessment, we might aim for a further four to eight weeks. That is an initial planning range, not a commitment before the technical and operational owners have reviewed it. We would prepare customer communications, support scripts, monitoring and rollback criteria before release.

Before the pilot, I’d agree what would justify **expanding, changing or stopping** it. Measures should include completion and abandonment for eligible customers, differences across relevant customer groups, service contacts, complaints, and fraud and false-positive signals. Where feasible, we should compare with a similar group, not attribute every change to the pilot. I’d also measure time from an agreed decision to release, so we learn whether the operating approach actually removes delay.

The consulting support I’d value is help with the evidence, journey and dependency mapping, and a practical decision-rights and capacity plan—not another committee or a strategy deck that ends before delivery. At the end, we should have a dated recommendation on the pilot and what, if anything, is worth applying to another journey.

Account opening is a plausible example, but we need evidence before selecting it.","target":"" , "images":null},{"type":"TALK","content":"I’d propose a project that tests a better way of delivering **one customer journey**, rather than a bank-wide transformation program.

**Possible starting point:** digital account opening. For example, if our data shows that customers get stuck during identity verification, we could explore whether they can resume the process or get help without starting again. That is a hypothesis, not a diagnosis: another journey may be a better candidate once we look at the evidence. Any change would retain the required identity and fraud controls.

I’d structure the work in three stages:

1. **Diagnose and select — approximately two weeks.** Map the actual journey, including branch and call-center handoffs. Review abandonment, complaints and service contacts; speak to customers and frontline staff. Identify the critical platform and policy dependencies, their owners, and where decisions or work are waiting. Establish a baseline and select a problem small enough to test.

2. **Agree the release — approximately two weeks.** The product lead would be accountable for the customer outcome, but platform, fraud, compliance and service owners would retain their own decisions. Together we would agree a bounded change, eligibility, required capacity, safeguards and an escalation path. If shared capacity cannot be committed, the relevant executives need to decide what moves—not leave the product team with an unsupported date.

3. **Deliver and assess a controlled pilot.** Depending on the dependency assessment, we might aim for a further four to eight weeks. That is an initial planning range, not a commitment before the technical and operational owners have reviewed it. We would prepare customer communications, support scripts, monitoring and rollback criteria before release.

Before the pilot, I’d agree what would justify **expanding, changing or stopping** it. Measures should include completion and abandonment for eligible customers, differences across relevant customer groups, service contacts, complaints, and fraud and false-positive signals. Where feasible, we should compare with a similar group, not attribute every change to the pilot. I’d also measure time from an agreed decision to release, so we learn whether the operating approach actually removes delay.

The consulting support I’d value is help with the evidence, journey and dependency mapping, and a practical decision-rights and capacity plan—not another committee or a strategy deck that ends before delivery. Ranking: E, C, B, D, A

Justification: The audio-only app would be my first pick. Ten bucks is a manageable way to try it, and Mira could make up stories without needing another screen to look at. I like audiobooks myself, and I can see us having fun coming up with ideas together.

The app with pictures is next. I’m a designer, so I definitely appreciate illustrations, and they could be a great part of the experience. I’d just prefer audio most of the time.

I’d choose no AI storyteller over buying either dedicated device. They sound fun, but a single-purpose gadget costing as much as a low-end phone or tablet is a lot for our budget. We’d be fine with library books and regular audiobooks instead.

Of the two devices, I’d put the audio-only one ahead because it keeps things simple and screen-free. The illustrated one is appealing too, but I don’t think I’d spend that much for the pictures.

Whichever option I tried, I’d want to listen with Mira at first and understand what happens to her voice or other information, including whether I could delete it. I wouldn’t just take ‘no supervision needed’ on faith.

I’d start with two ideas for Word:

1. **A living design brief.** Word could connect a project’s requirements, floor plans, specifications and applicable local regulations. If a layout changes, it could flag consequences throughout the document—for example, a bathroom arrangement that may no longer meet an accessibility requirement—and show the relevant drawing, rule and assumptions side by side. An architect would still review the finding, but the document would help us catch conflicts before they travel into construction.

2. **A design trade-off studio.** Starting from a brief, Word could generate and compare alternative apartment configurations or material assemblies. For each option, it could show indicative costs, embodied carbon, durability and effects on usable space, with the evidence and uncertainties behind each estimate. We could explore a change without committing to it, then carry the selected option through the specifications and diagrams.

The second idea particularly appeals to me: it makes the conversation about quality and cost much more concrete. Could a similar approach help with choices and uncertainty in your fields?
